Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

impose verb

lay a burden, a task, a rule or a penalty on someone

also impose a rule, impose a penalty, impose a burden, lay on, force on, saddle with

classical

Cic. Att. 13.11.1: nē magnum onus observantiae Brūtō nostrō impōnerem (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Phil. 7.15: lēgēs cīvitātī per vim imposuit (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 180: vectīgal impōnere

impōnō, impōnere, imposuī, impositum

verb, third conjugation: the thing in the accusative, the person in the dative

lay on, impose (a burden, a task, a law, a tax)

Literally to put on or into (a load on an animal, a pot on the fire); of burdens, tasks, laws, names and taxes the same. With a dative alone it also means to deceive: Catōnī ēgregiē imposuit Milō noster (Cic. Q. Fr. 2.6.5, Lewis & Short), “our Milo took Cato in beautifully”. So “I don’t want to impose on you” is not tibi impōnere: see impose on.

Other words

  • injungō, injungere, injūnxī, injūnctum — lay on, enjoin (a task, a burden, a duty)

    verb, third conjugation: the thing in the accusative, the person in the dative · also used · classical · Liv. 5.4.3: novum labōrem (Lewis & Short); Liv. 26.35.9: onus (Lewis & Short)

    Literally to join or fasten into; Lewis & Short gives impōnō as its synonym in this sense. Livy’s word, and Pliny’s for a task one is given.

Examples

  • nē magnum onus observantiae Brūtō nostrō impōnerem

    so as not to impose on our Brutus the great burden of attending on meCic. Att. 13.11.1 (Lewis & Short)

  • lēgēs cīvitātī per vim imposuit

    he imposed laws on the state by forceCic. Phil. 7.15 (Lewis & Short)

  • Catōnī ēgregiē imposuit Milō noster

    our Milo took Cato in beautifully (impōnere with a dative alone: deceive)Cic. Q. Fr. 2.6.5 (Lewis & Short)

  • Nōlī puerō plūs oneris impōnere quam ferre potest.

    Don’t put more on the boy than he can carry.composed

See also tax, impose on, trick, rule.

SourcesLewis & Short: impono · Lewis & Short: injungo

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 180.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
